name: (CS)²AI Online™ Symposium: Cybersecurity of Smart Buildings
description:
### Panel A: When Hackers Cross into the Physical World — Ransomware and Building Systems

**Description:**
Attackers are no longer content with stealing data. In 2026 they have hacked refrigeration systems across hundreds of grocery stores, causing spoiled food and fires. They have disrupted door access and HVAC at a hospital, and they have locked staff out of their own offices to force ransom payments. Building automation systems (BAS) control HVAC, access control, lighting, elevators and fire panels. Most of them run on protocols with no authentication, and they are rarely monitored. That makes them both leverage for extortion and a hidden way into corporate IT. This panel looks at how and why attackers target buildings, what a “physical consequence” attack looks like, and what owners, operators and integrators should do now.

### Presentation: Managing Smart Building Vendors: Practical Strategies to Reduce Cybersecurity and Operational Risk

***

### Panel B: Smarter Buildings, Smarter Attackers — AI, Regulation and Accountability

**Description:**
AI is entering building operations from both directions. Operators are deploying AI agents to optimize energy, comfort and maintenance. Attackers are using AI to learn obscure embedded systems and speed up reconnaissance. At the same time, regulation is catching up: NIS2 and the EU Cyber Resilience Act are bringing BAS into compliance scope. Insurers are demanding evidence of controls, and boards are being told that cyber risk to physical operations is a governance issue. This panel examines what AI changes in building cybersecurity, how emerging rules affect owners, manufacturers and integrators, and who should be accountable when a “smart” building is compromised.

Agentic engineering only works if the platform underneath it can support autonomous action safely. 1. How to build a controlled action layer that exposes approved capabilities to agents through APIs, Infrastructure as Code, and GitOps rather than direct infrastructure access.
2. How to give each agent an identity, scoped permissions, and explicit boundaries so autonomy stays bounded and humans approve what matters.
3. How to close the feedback loop with observability, testing, policy checks, SLOs, and audit data so agents know whether an action worked and can respond when it didn't.

name: Building Privacy Preserving Token Applications Using Panurus
description:
Panurus ([https://github.com/LFDT-Panurus](https://github.com/LFDT-Panurus)) is an open-source framework for building token-based applications that preserve transactional privacy while remaining fully auditable and interoperable across ledgers. In this talk, we'll walk through how Panurus's driver-based architecture lets developers plug in different token technologies — from Fabtoken to zero-knowledge schemes — behind a common transaction lifecycle (Request → Assemble → Sign → Commit), and how this enables privacy-preserving applications without locking you into a single blockchain or cryptographic scheme.

We'll also spotlight two mentorship programs currently pushing Panurus's capabilities forward:

**\- EVM Network Driver** — extending Panurus with support for EVM-compatible chains, bringing privacy-preserving tokens to Ethereum and its ecosystem.
**\- zkat\-snark Driver** — introducing a zk-SNARK-based anonymous token driver, expanding Panurus's toolkit for confidential, provably-correct transactions.

Come see how these efforts are shaping Panurus's roadmap, and how you can get involved.

description:
When infrastructure fails or drifts, resolution still looks like it did a decade ago: a human reads logs, pieces together what changed and hand-writes a fix. Artem Artyunov of env zero demos a different path: an AI coding assistant and a custom skill from Git, asking a live IaC platform which environments failed, what drifted and what the safe fix is.

We'll cover:
1\. Asking plain-language questions of a live infrastructure-as-code platform through its CLI, using an AI coding assistant and a custom skill loaded from Git.
2\. See how the skill is built, and how authentication and guardrails keep the agent from doing anything you didn't approve.
3\. A working pattern you can adapt to your own IaC tooling, and a realistic view of what agentic remediation can and can't do today, including where human review still belongs.

name: Tame PyTorch Recompiles & Unlock Jev GPU Throughput with Zymtrace
description:
**Monday, November 16, 2026 · 9:00–10:00 AM PST · Online**
**Zoom link:** [https://us02web.zoom.us/j/82308186562](https://us02web.zoom.us/j/82308186562)
Join us for two deep dives into hidden AI performance costs: surprise PyTorch recompilations during inference and compute, memory, and communication bottlenecks in Jev training.
**Talk #0: Introductions and Meetup Updates**
by Chris Fregly and Antje Barth
**Talk #1: Overcoming the PyTorch Recompilation Dilemma in Real-Time Inference Workloads**
by Chaim Rand
`torch.compile` can accelerate steady-state inference, yet a guard failure on a new input shape or layout can trigger an expensive recompilation in the request path. Drawing on his latest post, Chaim will compare six approaches using a dynamic graph-neural-network example: cache preloading, bounded recompilation with eager fallback, Dynamo and input-layout tuning, warmup seeding, background compilation, and ahead-of-time compilation with `torch.export` and AOTInductor. He’ll explain their tradeoffs and how the right choice depends on the model, input distribution, runtime environment, and latency requirements.
**Bio:** Chaim Rand is a machine-learning algorithm developer who writes about PyTorch and practical AI/ML performance optimization.
**Based on:** [Overcoming the PyTorch Recompilation Dilemma in Real-Time Inference Workloads](https://chaimrand.medium.com/overcoming-the-pytorch-recompilation-dilemma-in-real-time-inference-workloads-069fac5485cd)
**Talk #2: From Profiles to Throughput: How TypeSafe Optimized Jev with Zymtrace**
by Israel Ogbole, Co-founder and CEO of Zymtrace
Israel will explore the latest Zymtrace/TypeSafe case study on training and serving Jev. He’ll discuss how continuous CPU/GPU profiling and MCP-accessible profile data supported an iterative optimization loop across compute, memory, communication, and inference synchronization. The published case study reports approximately 46% higher training throughput on the same hardware after three successive changes, plus approximately 10% better inference performance after removing a hidden device-to-host synchronization. The talk will focus on how the team found each bottleneck, measured each change, and identified the next constraint.
**Bio:** Israel Ogbole is co-founder and CEO of Zymtrace, which develops continuous CPU/GPU profiling tools for performance optimization.
**Based on:** [How TypeSafe achieved 46% higher GPU throughput training Jev — with the help of Zymtrace](https://zymtrace.com/article/typesafe-zymtrace/)
